question: Before loading or unloading Class 1 (Explosives) materials, what must a driver do?
choice_a: Turn off the engine, disable cargo heaters, disconnect heater power sources, and drain heater fuel tanks
choice_b: Leave the engine running to keep the cargo heater on
choice_c: Open all cargo heater vents for ventilation
choice_d: Only disconnect the truck battery
explanation: The manual states you must turn your engine off before loading or unloading explosives, then check the cargo space, disable cargo heaters, disconnect heater power sources, and drain heater fuel tanks.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, Subsection 9.4, Loading and Unloading, Precautions for Specific Hazards (Class 1 Explosives)

question: Why must Class 4 (Flammable Solids) and Class 5 (Oxidizing) materials be kept dry during loading, unloading, and transit?
choice_a: Because water reduces their shelf life only
choice_b: Because moisture voids their shipping papers
choice_c: Because they must be weighed before shipment
choice_d: Because they become unstable and dangerous when wet
explanation: Class 4 and 5 materials, which become unstable and dangerous when wet, must be kept dry while in transit and during loading and unloading.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, Subsection 9.4, Loading and Unloading, Precautions for Specific Hazards (Class 4 and 5 Materials)

question: When loading breakable containers of corrosive liquid by hand, how should they be loaded?
choice_a: Rolled gently into place to save time
choice_b: One by one, right side up, without dropping or rolling them
choice_c: Upside down to prevent spilling from the cap
choice_d: Several at a time stacked on their sides
explanation: If loading by hand, load breakable containers of corrosive liquid one by one, keep them right side up, and do not drop or roll the containers.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, Subsection 9.4, Loading and Unloading, Precautions for Specific Hazards (Class 8 Corrosive Materials)

question: According to the manual, nitric acid must never be loaded in what manner?
choice_a: In the front of the cargo space
choice_b: Below any other product
choice_c: Above any other product
choice_d: Next to empty containers
explanation: The manual specifically states: 'Do not load nitric acid above any other product.'
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, Subsection 9.4, Loading and Unloading, Precautions for Specific Hazards (Class 8 Corrosive Materials)

question: What precautions must be taken when loading charged storage batteries?
choice_a: Only load them with other charged batteries
choice_b: Load them upside down to prevent terminal contact
choice_c: Discharge them fully before loading
choice_d: Load them so their liquid won't spill, keep them right side up, and make sure other cargo won't fall against or short circuit them
explanation: Charged storage batteries must be loaded so their liquid won't spill, kept right side up, with other cargo prevented from falling against or short circuiting them.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, Subsection 9.4, Loading and Unloading, Precautions for Specific Hazards (Class 8 Corrosive Materials)

question: Per the manual, corrosive liquids must never be loaded next to or above materials from which of these classes?
choice_a: Class 9 (Miscellaneous Hazardous Materials)
choice_b: Non-hazardous general freight
choice_c: Division 4.3 (Dangerous When Wet materials)
choice_d: Division 6.2 (Infectious Substances)
explanation: The manual lists Division 4.3 (Dangerous When Wet), along with Division 1.4, Division 4.1, Class 5, and Division 2.3 Zone B, as materials that must never be loaded next to or above corrosive liquids.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, Subsection 9.4, Loading and Unloading, Precautions for Specific Hazards (Class 8 Corrosive Materials)

question: If a vehicle carrying compressed gas cylinders has no racks to hold them, what is required?
choice_a: The cargo space floor must be flat, and cylinders must be held upright or secured in racks or boxes that prevent turnover
choice_b: Cylinders may be stacked freely without restraint
choice_c: The cargo space must be refrigerated
choice_d: Cylinders must always be loaded lying flat regardless of valve position
explanation: If a vehicle doesn't have racks to hold cylinders, the cargo space floor must be flat, and the cylinders must be held upright or in racks/boxes attached to the vehicle that keep them from turning over.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, Subsection 9.4, Loading and Unloading, Precautions for Specific Hazards (Class 2 Compressed Gases)

question: A package labeled POISON or POISON INHALATION HAZARD must never be loaded where?
choice_a: Next to other Division 6.1 packages
choice_b: In the driver's cab or sleeper, or with food material for human or animal consumption
choice_c: In the rearmost part of an enclosed trailer
choice_d: On top of Class 8 corrosive materials only
explanation: The manual states you must never load a package labeled POISON or POISON INHALATION HAZARD in the driver's cab or sleeper, or with food material for human or animal consumption.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, Subsection 9.4, Loading and Unloading, Precautions for Specific Hazards (Division 2.3/6.1 Poisonous Materials)

question: What is the maximum total transport index of all Class 7 (Radioactive) packages allowed in a single vehicle?
explanation: The manual states the total transport index of all packages in a single vehicle must not exceed 50.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, Subsection 9.4, Loading and Unloading, Precautions for Specific Hazards (Class 7 Radioactive Materials)

question: Per the manual's example, how close to people or cargo space walls can a package with a transport index of 1.1 be loaded?
choice_a: There is no distance restriction for a transport index of 1.1
choice_b: It must be at least six inches away
choice_c: It cannot be within two feet of people or cargo space walls
choice_d: It cannot be within ten feet of people or cargo space walls
explanation: The manual gives the example that you can't leave a package with a transport index of 1.1 within two feet of people or cargo space walls.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, Subsection 9.4, Loading and Unloading, Precautions for Specific Hazards (Class 7 Radioactive Materials)

topic: Do Not Load Table - Poison with Food
question: According to the Do Not Load table, Division 6.1 or 2.3 poison-labeled material must not be loaded with animal or human food unless what?
choice_a: The poison package weighs less than 50 pounds
choice_b: The poison package is over-packed in an approved way
choice_c: The shipper signs a waiver
choice_d: The food is in refrigerated containers
explanation: The Do Not Load table (Figure 9.9) states poison or poison inhalation hazard labeled material must not be loaded with food unless the poison package is over-packed in an approved way; mouthwash, toothpaste, and skin creams are not considered foodstuffs.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, Subsection 9.4, Do Not Load Table (Figure 9.9)

topic: Do Not Load Table - Detonating Primers
question: Per the Do Not Load table, Class 1 detonating primers must not be loaded with other explosives unless what condition is met?
choice_a: The primers are inert
choice_b: The other explosives are Division 1.4 only
choice_c: They are in authorized containers or packages
choice_d: They are shipped by a different carrier
explanation: The Do Not Load table states Class 1 detonating primers must not be loaded with any other explosives unless in authorized containers or packages.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, Subsection 9.4, Do Not Load Table (Figure 9.9)

question: Per the Do Not Load table, Division 6.1 cyanides or cyanide mixtures (such as Sodium Cyanide) must not be loaded with which materials?
choice_a: Acids, corrosive materials, or other acidic materials which could release hydrocyanic acid
choice_b: Combustible liquids of any kind
choice_c: Explosives of Division 1.4 only
choice_d: Any Class 9 miscellaneous hazardous material
explanation: The Do Not Load table lists cyanides (such as Cyanides Inorganic n.o.s., Silver Cyanide, Sodium Cyanide) as unable to be loaded with acids, corrosive materials, or other acidic materials which could release hydrocyanic acid.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, Subsection 9.4, Do Not Load Table (Figure 9.9)

question: According to the manual, what best describes a cargo tank?
choice_a: A packaging removed from the vehicle for filling before being placed back on
choice_b: A non-bulk packaging used only for solids
choice_c: Any container holding less than 119 gallons
choice_d: Bulk packaging permanently attached to a vehicle that remains on the vehicle when loaded and unloaded
explanation: Cargo tanks are bulk packaging permanently attached to a vehicle. Cargo tanks remain on the vehicle when you load and unload them.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, Subsection 9.5, Bulk Packaging Marking, Loading and Unloading

question: How do portable tanks differ from cargo tanks according to the manual?
choice_a: There is no difference; the terms are interchangeable
choice_b: Portable tanks are always smaller than 100 gallons
choice_c: Portable tanks are not permanently attached to a vehicle; the product is loaded or unloaded while the tank is off the vehicle
choice_d: Portable tanks can never hold liquids
explanation: Portable tanks are bulk packaging that are not permanently attached to a vehicle. The product is loaded or unloaded while the portable tanks are off the vehicle, then the tanks are put on a vehicle for transportation.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, Subsection 9.5, Bulk Packaging Marking, Loading and Unloading

question: How must identification numbers be displayed on portable tanks, cargo tanks, and other bulk packaging?
choice_a: As black 100 mm (3.9 inch) numbers on orange panels, placards, or a white diamond-shaped background if no placards are required
choice_b: Embossed directly into the metal only
choice_c: Handwritten in permanent marker anywhere visible
choice_d: As red numbers on a blue background
explanation: The rules require black 100 mm (3.9 inch) numbers on orange panels, placards, or a white, diamond-shaped background if no placards are required.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, Subsection 9.5.1, Markings

topic: Portable Tank ID Placement, Large Tanks
question: On a portable tank or other bulk packaging holding 1,000 gallons or more, where must the identification number appear?
choice_a: On two opposing sides only
choice_b: On each side and each end
choice_c: On the top only
choice_d: On the bottom only
explanation: The identification number must appear on each side and each end of a portable tank or other bulk packaging that holds 1,000 gallons or more.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, Subsection 9.5.1, Markings

question: The person watching the loading or unloading of a cargo tank must be within how many feet of the tank?
choice_a: 100 feet
choice_b: 10 feet
choice_c: 25 feet
choice_d: 50 feet
explanation: The person watching the loading or unloading must be within 25 feet of the tank, among other duties.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, Subsection 9.5.2, Tank Loading

question: What must be done before moving a cargo tank of hazardous materials, no matter how small the amount in the tank?
choice_a: Close all manholes and valves
choice_b: Notify the National Response Center
choice_c: Empty the tank completely
choice_d: Remove all placards
explanation: Manholes and valves must be closed before moving a tank of hazardous materials, no matter how small the amount, to prevent leaks.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, Subsection 9.5.2, Tank Loading

question: When loading a cargo tank with a flammable liquid through an open filling hole, what must be done regarding grounding?
choice_a: Grounding is only required for gases, not liquids
choice_b: Grounding is optional if the engine is off
choice_c: Ground the tank before opening the filling hole and maintain the ground until after closing it
choice_d: Ground the tank only after the filling hole is closed
explanation: The manual states to ground the tank before opening the filling hole, and maintain the ground until after closing the filling hole.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, Subsection 9.5.3, Flammable Liquids

question: A vehicle carrying Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives must never be parked within how many feet of the traveled part of the road?
choice_a: Fifty feet
choice_b: One hundred feet
choice_c: Fifteen feet
choice_d: Five feet
explanation: The manual states never park with Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives within five feet of the traveled part of the road.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, Subsection 9.6.1, Parking with Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 Explosives

question: Except for short periods needed for vehicle operation necessities such as fueling, a vehicle loaded with Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives must not be parked within 300 feet of which of the following?
choice_a: A bridge, tunnel, or building
choice_b: A state highway sign
choice_c: An empty parking lot
choice_d: A rest area with no other vehicles
explanation: The manual states not to park within 300 feet of a bridge, tunnel, or building; a place where people gather; or an open fire, except for short necessary periods.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, Subsection 9.6.1, Parking with Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 Explosives

question: What is a 'safe haven' as described in the manual?
choice_a: A fireproof storage warehouse
choice_b: The shipper's loading dock only
choice_c: Any rest area along the interstate
choice_d: An approved place for parking unattended vehicles loaded with explosives, usually designated by local authorities
explanation: A safe haven is an approved place for parking unattended vehicles loaded with explosives, with designation of authorized safe havens usually made by local authorities.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, Subsection 9.6.1, Parking with Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 Explosives

topic: Parking a Placarded Vehicle Without Explosives
question: You may park a placarded vehicle (not carrying explosives) within five feet of the traveled part of the road under what condition?
choice_a: Only between the hours of 10 p.m. and 6 a.m.
choice_b: Anytime it is convenient
choice_c: Only if the vehicle is empty
choice_d: Only if your work requires it, and only briefly, with someone always watching the vehicle
explanation: You may park a placarded vehicle not laden with explosives within five feet of the traveled part of the road only if your work requires it, only briefly, and someone must always watch the vehicle.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, Subsection 9.6.2, Parking a Placarded Vehicle Not Transporting Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 Explosives

question: The person attending a placarded vehicle must be in the vehicle, awake, and not in the sleeper berth, or within how many feet of the vehicle with it in clear view?
choice_a: 100 feet
choice_b: 500 feet
choice_c: 25 feet
choice_d: 300 feet
explanation: The person attending must be in the vehicle, awake, and not in the sleeper berth, or within 100 feet of the vehicle and have it within clear view.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, Subsection 9.6.3, Attending Parked Vehicles

question: Around which of the following must a driver never use burning signals such as flares or fuses?
choice_a: An empty flatbed trailer
choice_b: A vehicle carrying only non-hazardous general freight
choice_c: A refrigerated trailer
choice_d: A tank used for Class 3 (Flammable Liquids) or Division 2.1 (Flammable Gas), whether loaded or empty
explanation: The manual states you must never use burning signals, such as flares or fuses, around a tank used for Class 3 or Division 2.1 materials, whether loaded or empty, or a vehicle loaded with Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, Subsection 9.6.4, No Flares!

question: If transporting Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives, what must the driver have and follow?
choice_a: A copy of the shipper's insurance policy
choice_b: A written route plan
choice_c: A verbal agreement with the dispatcher only
choice_d: Only a GPS device
explanation: If transporting Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives, you must have a written route plan and follow that plan; carriers prepare the plan in advance for company terminals, or the driver may plan the route if picking up elsewhere.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, Subsection 9.6.5, Route Restrictions

question: A driver must not smoke within how many feet of a placarded cargo tank used for Class 3 (Flammable Liquids) or Division 2.1 (Gases)?
choice_a: 100 feet
choice_b: 25 feet
choice_c: 300 feet
choice_d: 10 feet
explanation: The manual states do not smoke within 25 feet of a placarded cargo tank used for Class 3 (flammable liquids) or Division 2.1 (gases).
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, Subsection 9.6.6, No Smoking

question: What is required when fueling a motor vehicle containing hazardous materials?
choice_a: Fuel only at night
choice_b: Keep the engine running to maintain electrical systems
choice_c: Turn off the engine, and have someone always at the nozzle controlling fuel flow
choice_d: No special precautions are required
explanation: The manual states to turn off your engine before fueling a motor vehicle containing hazardous materials, and someone must always be at the nozzle, controlling fuel flow.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, Subsection 9.6.7, Refuel with Engine Off

question: The power unit of a placarded vehicle must have a fire extinguisher with what minimum UL rating?
choice_b: 10 B:C
choice_c: 5 B:C
choice_d: 20 A:B
explanation: The manual requires a fire extinguisher with a UL rating of 10 B:C or more on the power unit of placarded vehicles.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, Subsection 9.6.8, 10 B C Fire Extinguisher

question: When must a driver examine each tire on a motor vehicle carrying hazardous materials?
choice_a: At the beginning of each trip and each time the vehicle is parked
choice_b: Only once per week
choice_c: Only if a warning light appears
choice_d: Only before crossing state lines
explanation: The manual states you must examine each tire on a motor vehicle at the beginning of each trip and each time the vehicle is parked.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, Subsection 9.6.9, Check Tires

topic: Driving on a Leaking or Flat Tire
question: If a tire on a placarded vehicle is leaking or flat, when may you drive on it?
choice_a: Anywhere, as long as speed is reduced
choice_b: Never, the vehicle must be towed immediately
choice_c: Only on interstate highways
choice_d: Only to the nearest safe place to fix it
explanation: The manual states not to drive with a tire that is leaking or flat except to the nearest safe place to fix it.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, Subsection 9.6.9, Check Tires

question: While behind the wheel, where must hazardous materials shipping papers be kept?
choice_a: In the cargo area with the freight
choice_b: Within reach with your seat belt on, or in a pouch on the driver's door
choice_c: In the glove compartment only
choice_d: In the sleeper berth
explanation: The manual states that when behind the wheel, you must keep shipping papers within your reach (with your seat belt on), or in a pouch on the driver's door, easily seen by someone entering the cab.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, Subsection 9.6.10, Where to Keep Shipping Papers and Emergency Response Information

question: When not behind the wheel, where should the driver leave hazardous materials shipping papers?
choice_a: With the emergency response information removed
choice_b: In the driver's door pouch or on the driver's seat
choice_c: Locked in the trailer with the cargo
choice_d: Mailed to the carrier's terminal
explanation: The manual states that when not behind the wheel, leave shipping papers in the driver's door pouch or on the driver's seat.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, Subsection 9.6.10, Where to Keep Shipping Papers and Emergency Response Information

question: A driver transporting chlorine in cargo tanks must have what special equipment in the vehicle?
choice_a: A portable generator
choice_b: A fire hose and self-contained breathing apparatus
choice_c: An approved gas mask and an emergency kit for controlling leaks in dome cover plate fittings
choice_d: A second spare tire only
explanation: A driver transporting chlorine in cargo tanks must have an approved gas mask in the vehicle and an emergency kit for controlling leaks in dome cover plate fittings on the cargo tank.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, Subsection 9.6.11, Equipment for Chlorine

question: A placarded vehicle must stop how many feet before the nearest rail at a railroad crossing?
choice_a: 15 to 50 feet
choice_b: 5 to 10 feet
choice_c: 50 to 100 feet
choice_d: 100 to 200 feet
explanation: The manual states you must stop 15 to 50 feet before the nearest rail.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, Subsection 9.6.12, Stop before Railroad Crossings

question: The Emergency Response Guidebook (ERG) is indexed by what two things?
choice_a: Driver's license number and vehicle VIN
choice_b: Weight and dimensions of the package
choice_c: Carrier name and DOT number
choice_d: Proper shipping name and hazardous materials identification number
explanation: The guide is indexed by proper shipping name and hazardous materials identification number, which emergency personnel look for on the shipping paper.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, Subsection 9.7.1, Emergency Response Guidebook (ERG)

topic: Driver's Job at a Crash Scene
question: As a commercial driver, what is your job at the scene of a hazardous materials crash or incident?
choice_a: Keep people away, limit the spread of material only if you can safely do so, communicate the danger, and provide shipping papers and emergency response information to responders
choice_b: Wait inside the vehicle until police arrive without communicating
choice_c: Leave the scene to avoid liability
choice_d: Immediately begin cleaning up the spill yourself
explanation: The manual lists a driver's job at the scene as keeping people away, limiting the spread of material only if safe, communicating the danger to responders, and providing shipping papers and emergency response information.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, Subsection 9.7.2, Crashes/Incidents

question: Should a driver attempt to fight a hazardous materials fire?
choice_a: Yes, but only if the fire is small
choice_b: No, drivers should never call for help either
choice_c: No, unless the driver has the training and equipment to do so safely, since it requires special training and protective gear
choice_d: Yes, always, using the vehicle's fire extinguisher
explanation: Unless you have the training and equipment to do so safely, don't fight hazardous materials fires; dealing with them requires special training and protective gear.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, Subsection 9.7.3, Fires

question: Before opening trailer doors when a cargo fire is suspected, what should a driver do?
choice_a: Feel the doors; if they are hot, do not open them, since opening them lets air in and may make the fire flare up
choice_b: Spray water directly on the doors before opening
choice_c: Open the doors immediately to let smoke escape
choice_d: Kick the doors open to check for damage
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to feel trailer doors to see if they are hot before opening them; if hot, there may be a cargo fire, and doors should not be opened because it lets air in and may make the fire flare up.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, Subsection 9.7.3, Fires

question: Why should a driver never try to identify a leaking hazardous material by smell?
choice_a: Smelling the material voids the shipping papers
choice_b: It has no real risk, but wastes time
choice_c: Toxic gases can destroy your sense of smell and can injure or kill you even if they don't smell
choice_d: It is against federal regulations to smell any package
explanation: The manual warns that toxic gases can destroy your sense of smell and can injure or kill you even if they don't smell, so never try to identify the material or find the source of a leak by smell.
source_note: Massachusetts Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, base AAMVA content Version: July 2017, Massachusetts-specific front matter revised March 2025), Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles (RMV) -- Section 9, Hazardous Materials, Subsection 9.7.3, Fires

topic: Responding to a Hazardous Materials Spill
question: If hazardous materials are spilling from your vehicle, what should you do?
choice_a: Transfer the load to another vehicle on the roadway immediately
choice_b: Continue driving until you find a phone
